column8: I knew that this program was a bold experiment, and that the experiment might not necessarily meet my needs, and was okay with that--worse case, I'd eat well, enjoy Hollyhock grounds, hangout with good humans, get to relax. [I note that some of the other participants seemed very happy with the offering]. After going through it, and finding it wanting, I realized 1) I didn't interpret the offering correctly, so that's my fault and my disappointment was related to me visioning something else that was never the presenters' intended offering and; 2) there's possibly a flaw in the model. The presenters initial pitch read, "Why are we offering this opportunity? Interestingly, the inspiration for this retreat emerged from what might be called an "anti-retreat" experience. During a conference at Hollyhock, we both quietly confessed to each other that the most meaningful moments for us were not the structured sessions, but rather the unplanned, in-between moments when we would skip a workshop to take a brief swim in the ocean or simply enjoy unscheduled time. It became clear that we were taking mini-retreats within the retreat itself. And from this realization, the idea for the Collective Reset was born. We asked ourselves, between sips of tea and lots of laughs: “What if we designed a retreat entirely around these kinds of unstructured, in-between experiences?.”" I could relate to this -- I've experienced this at other conferences / workshops. But the key was the other people at the conference / workshop were all interested in very similar topics or worked in a similar area. So that meant that at coffee breaks, lunch, walks, etc, we would have shared interests to talk about, or we would talk about something that came up in a previous session, or we would benefit from networking. Also, our group was small, a 12 too small in my view to ensure that there'd be enough people whose work challenges and learnings were relevant to mine (three were people I learned from and would keep in touch with). Anyhow, I would have appreciated a little more structure, some more useful exercises, better pairing off / small group work. I also know how to relax, to get out in nature, to do yoga, connect with friends etc. Notwithstanding this, I benefited from the relaxation etc, I appreciate that the presenters were very well intentioned and I could see that others were apparently getting what they needed out of it.

See above about the facilitators!

Additionally, I had an unfortunate experience during a bodywork session with Andrew (my appt was Thurs 15 May at 4pm). The massage itself was great, but when I sat up from the massage table I noticed immediately that his cell phone had been left on the wooden shelf on the wall (alongside the speaker and essential oils) and was standing up such that the phone camera was pointed directly toward the massage table. Given that I was topless and only wearing underwear on the bottom, this was jarring and I immediately felt unsafe. At the time, I just got dressed and left the space. I didn’t touch the phone or look any closer so I have to assume that it was just left that way without any ill intent, but the impact was that it left me feeling vulnerable and uncomfortable. I didn’t pay attention to the shelf before the massage so I don’t know how long it had been like that. I did briefly mention this to the woman working in the shop when I checked out on Friday and said that it was still an overall good experience and that I mentioned this because it could easily be avoided for someone in the future. I’ve found myself still feeling upset about this after the weekend and needing to share the reality of the experience. The lack of care for safety in that moment tainted my experience not only of the appointment but to some degree my time at Hollyhock as well. As women, we spend so much of our time and energy existing in the world with concern for our safety and it was such a privilege to release that worry during my time on Cortes and at Hollyhock, so I found it upsetting to then be in a position to question that perceived safety. We are particularly vulnerable in a massage or bodywork setting, and the blind trust we offer to the person working with us is something that should never be taken lightly, especially in the instance of a male body worker and female client due to the inherent power differential. Just regarding the journey to and from. It would be great if you could provide a more accurate description of the travel difficulties and recommendations for either staying another night to avoid weekend returns or that one should leave very very early.

The travel to and from has been exceptionally difficult and time consuming. By way of example, I left my program early at 11 and missed my 545 reservation from Vancouver island  and was stuck waiting at the terminal where there was no food other than vending snacks for 5 hours and barely be got on as a standby for the 10:45 ferry to Vancouver as a standby (I was the 3rd to last car on—and then the ferry was delayed so did not arrive at Tsawassen until 2a). It would have been very helpful to know and I would have made other arrangements. Also perhaps letting people know there is no food at Duke Pt would be helpful. I also was late to the program despite leaving Vancouver at 10:15 because of ferry issues. It would have been good to provide information to suggest arriving 2 hours early for the smaller ferries, and suggestions about either bringing food in case one gets stuck or suggesting places to get a meal and kr stay—if I hadn’t gotten on the 10:45 for example, I would’ve been on the hunt for a hotel. Note that I was not the only one—another retreatant experienced the same thing, only she had no hotel in Tsawassen and hotels were booked. Fortunately I saw her at the hotel and was able to offer her to stay with me. She is 77 with mobility issues. The journey was already difficult for her—and not having this information, I imagine, made it more challenging.

I’d also suggest that there be either more information about how those with mobility issues get around the property. I saw my new friend struggle quite a bit. And I’d love for this to be addressed and for her and others like her to be able to come to such a magical place. 

Other than the travel issues, for me, the retreat center is lovely as are everyone who works there. Everything there was perfect.

It feels like Hollyhock is undergoing an identity crisis.   I have been coming for more than 20 years. Over the past 5-7 years HH seems to have lost its focus as sacred retreat space. 
During the last two retreats I attended, screaming children were often in the “spa” where the sign asks guests to “whisper or enjoy in silence”, while barking dogs were outside the spa space, tourists were walking talking around taking pictures, loud groups were drinking alcohol on the deck, and families were camping and children screaming well past 10pm in the once quiet and sacred forest camping sites.    I remember HH used to have family programs designed specifically for families.  I think that is a good idea to have separate adult-only and family retreats. As an adult expecting a sacred retreat space, I would like to know that the retreats I am signing up for are adult-only on campus.  The container is what makes retreat and transformation possible and right now,  It does not feel like anyone is intentionally creating and holding a retreat-space container at Hollyhock.  I am hopeful that the incoming leader will help repair what has been broken and create new sacred space for transformation.

I know I'm still fresh from this experience, but I can say with profound groundedness that participating in Margie Gillis' “Dancing from the Inside Out” program was one of the most cherished opportunities of my entire life.

I keep trying to place my finger on what exactly it was that set this so far apart, and it’s distillation is Union. Never have I had a teacher guide me so ease-fully back into my own soul’s expression. It touched on so much of what I grieve and reunited it with its joyous and gracious counterparts. It was a vow renewal to my aliveness and becoming in the most embodied way imaginable.

I have zero idea what any of my movements actually looked like; it will never matter. There was no choreography; no steps. Only improvisation. Texture. Energy. Only poetry, metaphor, storyline and abstract concept that somehow effortlessly uplifted technique and had me moving in ways that have long, longed to be freed from within. It felt like the best dancing of my life.

This is the prowess and blessing of a true Teacher—one who can see the subtlest thread and know exactly how to pull it so you break through to the other side, and who’s there to hold, catch, and witness you in the process. It’s long been my greatest goal to grow into this capacity in this lifetime, and I feel so honored to be graced by Margie’s 72 years on this Earth.

Through a seamless braid of somatics, reiki, and dance, Margie not only offered deep personal nourishment, but a practical toolbox of embodied practices for quite literally moving through the world—in our relationships, communities, art, and activism.

I feel so energized to pour this nourishment back out into others and confident in my capacity to hold my center and remain porous in the complexity of today's times.  

Thank you to Margie and her fantastic assistant teacher, Ruth Levin, for reminding us of why the revolution needs our joy.

column11: With over 20 people in our group, it would have been great to have incorporated some icebreakers early on. I've never been in such a group before where people were still asking one another their names after being together for 4 days. I wonder how attuned the presenter felt to the group during sessions, and whether there could be ways to adapt when it is sensed that participants might benefit from changing the format to encourage continued engagement. I think forming multiple circles at times would be supportive, whether it's 2 circles where the presenter and his assistant are each with a group--or trusting that participants can be on their own at times and have deeper conversations. Once in a while, it would be great to go around the circle to give everyone a chance to talk rather than popcorn style only. The program content was very interesting and the presenters did a phenomenal job - I appreciated being able to learn in a multitude of ways (dance, music, small groups, presentations, time in nature, etc.). The conversations and activities were magical to experience firsthand and I left Cortes feeling fulfilled and brimming with new perspectives, skills, and creative inspiration. The outdoor, nature and sound-based activities we very interesting to me - especially listening to the compost heap!

I loved all the group work and could imagine the program having even more small group discussions to break up some of the content and allow the group to get to know eachother more deeply. I found the long session on Zoom to be harder to connect with (versus having more in-person content).

As a BIPOC person, there were not many BIPOC voices in the space and it was a bit daunting to speak to my non-Western experiences - I am grateful that the presenters brought critical conversations about colonialism and other oppressive systems into the room, but it would have been interesting to have more group discussions on the topic (and of course more BIPOC folks in the room).

One of the most impactful experiences for me was the release ceremony we did in the ocean, accompanied by Pascal’s drumming. As we walked into the water, the rhythm of the drums and the support of the group created a powerful space for letting go of emotions and burdens I had been carrying. I felt a deep sense of release, clarity, and connection to myself, to the community, and to the natural world around us.

Malina Dawn’s guidance throughout this experience, weaving together Indigenous teachings and yoga, made the ceremony feel both sacred and transformative. It was a moment that reminded me of the power of ritual, presence, and reconnecting with joy and resilience even in challenging times.  After the ceremony, we all shared fresh oysters together, laughing and savoring the simple joy of being fully present a beautiful, grounding way to end such a powerful experience.
